'Big-game player': The spark igniting Ponga's finals charge
The Knights have backed Kalyn Ponga to continue his sensational run of form as they chase a historic victory in Sunday's semi-final at a sold-out Eden Park.
Newcastle have travelled to Auckland desperate to upset the Warriors in front of a record crowd and claim their first finals win in New Zealand.
It's been three years since the Knights last played a final across the Tasman, the Warriors prevailing 40-10 on that occasion.
Ponga's form this season has eclipsed that from 2023, in which he led Newcastle on a nine-game winning streak and charged to the Dally M Medal with a sensational finish to the year.
Kalyn Ponga: 'Connection to my heritage is strong'
Sunday's match provides a homecoming for the Māori All Star and centre Bradman Best said the fullback travelled to New Zealand with a steely look in his eye.
"He's grown into his leadership role," Best told NRL.com. "He's the captain of our club and what he's doing off the field is translating to the field.
"He's a big-game player and does a job every week. He's very consistent and fills the whole team with excitement and confidence. It's always good when he's running out in this form."

Queensland State of Origin honours followed but club success has been harder to come by.
That all changed this year, with new coach Justin Holbrook unlocking Ponga's lethal attacking skills in a high-octane system.

The fullback has 14 try assists and 12 linebreaks this season as the Knights went from wooden spooners to the most exciting team in the competition.
A laidback personality off the field, Ponga has faced criticism at times for his relaxed attitude but Best has noticed a new mindset in his captain throughout the season.
"He's pretty easy-going but he's taking his footy seriously," Best said. "He's really buying into it and leading by example. He's always putting his input in and talking up.
"He holds everyone to a higher standard, especially at training and on the field. That's showing and he's celebrating all the little wins. When we're playing under the bright lights he fills the boys up with a lot of confidence."

The fullback's presence takes the pressure of Sandon Smith and Fletcher Sharpe to create attacking opportunities, however they must remain switched on at all times and deliver him the football when demanded.
Holbrook: "This time of year is exciting"
The chance to play alongside Ponga was among the key factors in Smith's decision to join the Knights this year and he quickly noticed the positive impact on his own performances.
"Playing with [James Tedesco] was similar," Smith said. "You want the ball in your best player's hands as much as possible. One of my roles is to get Kalyn good ball and that's part of my job that I enjoy doing.
"When I create that space for Kalyn and then he sets up a try, I pat myself on the back knowing I contributed to that play for him. It's been awesome playing with a star player like that."

Immortal advice: How Johns helped Knights unlock attacking mindset
The words of NRL Immortal Andrew Johns will be ringing in the ears of Newcastle halfback Sandon Smith when he runs on to Eden Park for Sunday's sudden-death clash with the Warriors.
A two-time premiership winner and arguably the greatest No.7 to play the game, Johns' shadow has hung over the Knights since a neck injury forced him into retirement in 2007.
Success in Newcastle has been limited since their 2001 grand final victory and a host of halfbacks have struggled to handle the pressure that comes with following in an Immortal's footsteps.
Clive Churchill Medal winner: Andrew Johns - 2001
Johns hasn't shied away in his criticism of the club over the years but has embraced the current squad and has been a regular onlooker at training throughout the season.
The Immortal was on hand for the Knights captain's run prior to last week's elimination final victory over the Rabbitohs and Smith credited Johns for helping him handle the pressure on the big stage.
"It's awesome when he comes in," Smith told NRL.com. "He has a presence about him and an aura when he comes in and watches training. You know things are starting to heat up when he's coming in.
"This is when the big players step up and that's what Joey did throughout his career. This is our moment to prove to him and prove to everyone that we're a team like the Knights used to be."

items.body_excerpt:
Lucas races clock as Saturday deadline looms for comeback call
Dylan Lucas’ brave bid to return from a fractured ankle suffered in Round 21 has given Knights coach Justin Holbrook a selection headache he didn't expect to be facing.
Lucas was expected to miss the rest of the season after suffering the gruesome injury against the Roosters on July 24 - a horror night for the club which saw playmaker Dylan Brown do his ACL as well.
But Lucas has defied expectations to put himself in contention for Sunday’s sudden-death semi against the Warriors at Eden Park, with Holbrook praising the forward’s resilience and determination throughout his recovery.
“Everyone trained well. Obviously Dyl Lucas is the one we will see how he pulls up, and we won’t make a decision on him until Saturday,” Holbrook said.
“Credit to the medical staff and Dylan. The day he got injured he wanted to fast-track himself and do everything right.
“If he gets there on Sunday, we’ll all be happy for Dyl.”
Holbrook: "This time of year is exciting"
Lucas’ potential return would provide a major boost for the Knights but it would also leave the coach with a difficult decision after Francis Manuleleua and Jermaine McEwen have done an excellent job filling the void on the edges.
McEwen forced his way into the side during pre-season, while Manuleleua has made the most of his opportunity since Lucas’ injury.
“If I go all the way back to pre-season, they had a lot to work on and to their credit they have done that,” Holbrook said.
“Jermaine, from the start of the year, forced his way in, and now Francis, with his opportunity, has been outstanding for us.
“Both our back-rowers are doing a great job. We need them again to do that again Sunday. It's a bigger test again and I'm sure they will.”
The Lucas star is rising
For Holbrook, seeing players push to return from serious injuries and compete for their positions is a reflection of the culture developing within the group.
“It’s great as a coach to have players fighting to come back onto the field,” he said.
“It’s what you want to see with your group, and the boys are doing it.”
After overcoming South Sydney in an elimination final, Newcastle now faces a Warriors side on home soil, with Holbrook embracing the underdog tag once again.
“A lot of people thought we wouldn’t beat Souths, we did, and it’s similar again this week,” he said.
“But it’s different. You do get confidence, you have to be confident this time of year, but it’s a different challenge, a different game and different conditions.
“We’re confident that if we go over there and play well, we can get the win.”

Kirra v Jesse: You'll get a real kick out of this contest
Watching Jesse Southwell and Kirra Dibb put boot to ball in this Saturday’s elimination final between the Broncos and Knights will be a kickers’ field of dreams.
The two halfbacks can launch a Steeden with effortless ease.
Not only do they boast great positional and attacking kicks but they are the goalkickers for their respective clubs, ready to step up in big moments in finals.
In 2026, Southwell has her nose in front with 47 goals to Dibb's 40 and both have the same rate of accuracy at 84 per cent.
Across the final four rounds, Dibb nailed 21 shots at goal, including eight from 10 in a thumping 56-22 win over the Bulldogs in Round 10.
Southwell tuned up for the finals with seven from eight in last weekend's 52-18 win over the Warriors.
“They are both incredible players and I know they will each be on their best game because there is a nice rivalry there,” said Knights captain Kayla Romaniuk.
Broncos v Knights: Finals Week 1
“The kicking is where we’ll see it but there’s also how each half fits into their team structures and sets up plays.
“I’m excited to see them come up against each other.”
The pair are more than familiar with one another’s game – they helped win the Knights’ maiden NRLW premiership in 2022 as No.6 and No.7.
Another player who was part of that celebration was fullback Tamika Upton, now back at the Broncos and reunited with Southwell this year.
Jesse Southwell (centre) and Kirra Dibb (second from right) helped steer the Knights to glory in 2022.
“One thing I do know about Jesse is that she’s very diligent and very prepared for every game,” Upton told NRL.com.
“Nothing will change for her. Every single week you’d think she was playing in a grand final because of the way she prepares.
“There might be a bit of extra feeling being the old club but her only focus will be what she needs to do for our team because she’s a massive part of our team.”
Dibb’s return to the Knights after three years with the Cowboys has also brought the 29-year-old back into a NRLW finals campaign.
“Kirra has been amazing for us since she came back,” Romaniuk said. “I think she’s finally found her feet back with us and it’s so good to see her enjoying football again.”
Romaniuk came through the Newcastle pathways and played four NRLW seasons with Southwell.
“Jesse is always able to pull something out of nothing and that’s the threat she has. It is also the thing you can least prepare for,” Romaniuk said.
“We just have to stay connected in defence for whatever Jesse or their other strike players produce.
Kirra Dibb Try
“Kirra will definitely rise to the occasion because she has done it at finals time before and hasn’t been around finals for a few years.
“So it’s super-exciting for her to be back on this stage. Her kicking game has been outstanding this year.”
Upton also knows the Southwell game inside-out after three seasons at the Knights.
“She’s got to get me the ball the way that I like it and I’ve got to do my best in backing her up with what she’s trying to do,” Upton said.
What the two-time Dally M Medal winner has noticed in Southwell’s game is the influence of coach Scott Prince, himself a premiership-winning halfback with Wests Tigers (2005).

“One of the things Princey is so great at is instilling confidence in each player – ‘back your instincts’ is his motto," Upton said.
“He’s got Jesse running the ball a lot more. They also do (attacking) kicking sessions together and chat through the options.
“It’s great to see and this is not a one-year project.
“I’m very excited to see where Jesse's game goes.
“The kind of coach he is, he’s very attack-based and he’s freakishly good at it.”

'Test footy vibes': JFH embraces Eden Park magic
James Fisher-Harris knows what Eden Park can do to a team.
He has experienced the iconic stadium as a Kiwi international and watched the All Blacks turn it into one of the most intimidating fortresses in world rugby.
Now, with a sold-out crowd set to roar the Warriors on against Newcastle on Sunday, the veteran forward wants his men to create a piece of history of their own.
“I’ve played Kiwis here a couple of times,” Fisher-Harris said.
“Eden Park gives me Test footy vibes. Everything goes up a level for me personally.
“Watching the All Blacks do their thing here, it’s definitely a fortress for them."
The Warriors' last game at Eden Park back in 2014, when they dismantled the Raiders 54-12 thanks to a 26-point haul from Shaun Johnson.
More than a decade later, they return for a much bigger occasion, a do-or-die semi-final with a place in a preliminary final against the Panthers on the line.
Johnson goes 90 metres
And the timing could not be more fitting for a Warriors side that has spent 2026 rewriting the record books.
Andrew Webster’s men won 18 of their 24 regular-season games, setting a new club record and surpassing the previous benchmark of 17 wins in 2002 when the Wahs won their only minor premiership.
And Sunday’s clash is expected to smash New Zealand’s rugby league attendance record, with more than 48,000 fans set to pack into Eden Park - surpassing the previous record which has stood for almost 38 years of 47,363 for the Rugby League World Cup final at Eden Park on October 9, 1988.
Webster soaking up the Eden Park experience
For Fisher-Harris, though, one moment from the Warriors’ breakout season stands above the rest.
It came earlier in the year when the team performed the haka before their clash with his former club the Panthers.
Which they backed up with a statement 28-12 victory.
“There’s been some good games and finals-like games that I like playing in,” Fisher-Harris said.
“And probably one that comes to mind is when we did the haka here that trumps everything, because of the haka and the performance we backed up.
“I think that’s No.1.”
The Warriors have already created plenty of history this season.
But Fisher-Harris believes the biggest chapter is still to come.
“There’s been a lot of history this year, lots of pieces to the puzzle,” he said.
The Warriors’ loss to the Dolphins last week means they now have to take the longer route to the grand final.
James Fisher-Harris Try
And co-captain Fisher-Harris wants the Warriors to find the ruthlessness that was missing in their opening finals match and produce their best football when it matters most.
“The big thing is winning our little moments, not thinking too far ahead,” he said.
“I think we still haven’t found our best game yet. We are still chasing that.
“Great opportunity for us that we have put ourselves into this situation from being consistent heading into this weekend.
“Ruthlessness, we missed it on the weekend.
James Fisher-Harris got a taste of the Eden Park vibe at training this week. ©Photosport
“I’m keen to play our best game.”
The Warriors have the home-ground advantage to get them over the line, with the ultimate prize just three wins away.
“Personally and for the team’s sake, it’s the last game on home soil, so it’s definitely something to play for."
“We are going to leave it all out there.
“Not fuss about the result, but more about the performance.”

items.body_excerpt:
Webster draws on Panthers lessons as Wahs take 'scenic route' to prelim
Andrew Webster knows losing your opening finals game does not have to be the end of the road.
In fact, he has seen first-hand how taking the scenic route can lead to something even more special.
Webster was sitting alongside Ivan Cleary in the coaches’ box in Townsville when Penrith suffered a 16-10 loss to the Rabbitohs in their opening finals game in 2021, only to bounce back against the Eels and Storm before exacting the ultimate revenge on Southsin the grand final to launch a dynasty that would deliver four straight premierships.
That was the last time an NRL team has lost week one of finals and bounced back to win the grand final, which only five other teams since 1998 have achieved.
Now, five years on, Webster is drawing on those lessons as his Warriors attempt to write their own piece of history after losing 26-16 to the Dolphins in last week's qualifying final.
“We lost to Souths in North Queensland because it was COVID [in 2021] and I remember being disappointed, but just how positive everyone was about the next challenge,” Webster said.
Warriors v Dolphins - Finals Week 1, 2026
“We had to play Parra the next week, Melbourne the week after and ended up facing Souths in the grand final.”
The Warriors must now take the hard road if they are to claim an historic premiership but Webster believes that only makes the destination even sweeter.
“We are taking a different path now,” he said.
“It’s not the same one, it’s not the direct one, it’s scenic, going by the water, getting an ocean view.
Webster soaking up the Eden Park experience
“But once you achieve and get to your destination, it’s probably more enjoyable."
There is no shortage of belief inside the Warriors camp.
Despite being plunged into sudden-death after their loss to the Dolphins, Webster has maintained the positivity that he witnessed at Penrith five years ago.
The Knights now stand between New Zealand and another week of finals, having eliminated South Sydney 20-10 last weekend.
The two sides know each other well, having met only four weeks ago, but Webster is expecting a different challenge, with both teams playing to keep their dream alive.
“We were disappointed we lost, we wanted to win, we've got to move on quickly, we've got a new challenge," he said.
“If we win this week we are back where we wanted to be, and that’s in a grand final qualifier.
From the field: James Fisher-Harris
“We get to come here with the biggest crowd in Warriors history on New Zealand soil. Why would you be sulking? You would just be excited.
“A lot of history. It’s a special place."
Webster was impressed by what he saw from Newcastle against the Rabbitohs, particularly the attacking threats scattered across the field.
“They have got a threat and speed everywhere,” he said.
“Watching their finals game last week, I thought they were dominant.”
And the Warriors could receive another boost, with veteran winger Dallin Watene-Zelezniak named in the extended squad as he continues his bid to return from a broken collarbone.
The 31-year-old has not played since Round 25 but is desperate to force his way back into the side.
DWZ gets three
Webster knows the hurdles are significant but has been impressed by Watene-Zelezniak’s determination.
“He’s inspirational Dal, he’s fearless, he just wants to play so badly for the team,” Webster said.
“I’ve had to hold him back a bit to calm down. He’s saying, ‘Nup, give me an opportunity'.
“He’s got to tick a lot of boxes. The science is probably against him and he might not get there, but we will give him every chance.”

The New Zealand Warriors have confirmed Jackson Ford's latest injury will not finish his season if the Warriors can continue to stay alive in the NRL finals.

Sunday's Eden Park showdown against the Knights is a must-win for the Warriors.
Denied a trip straight to the preliminary finals last week after the Dolphins toppled them 26-16 at home, a loss to the Knights this weekend will end the Warriors' season - one that saw them finish second in the regular season – only pipped by the Panthers on points difference.
1News sports reporter Zion Dayal spoke to Channel Nine Australia rugby league reporter Zac Bailey ahead of Sunday's clash, discussing the Warriors' chances.
He tipped the Knights to ruin the party for Warriors fans, but said it could go either way.
"I don't know why. Just in the moment, I thought, you know what, the way the Knights beat the Bunnies, I was really impressed with. They're going to have to bring that again.
"I wanted it to be a Panthers-Warriors Grand Final. We won't get that now. Hopefully it's a Panthers-Warriors prelim final."
Bailey said the loss to the Dolphins will "make the job a lot harder". Only two teams have lost in week one of the finals and gone all the way – the Cowboys in 2015 and the Panthers in 2021.

"You basically can't hear yourself."

"This is just going to be like the Mount Smart or Go Media Stadium field on steroids, not only for the Knights players, but also for the Wahs players."

items.title: The 'forgotten' match: Why Eden Park boss was wrong about NZ's biggest league occasion - NZ Herald
items.snippet: The 'forgotten' match: Why Eden Park boss was wrong about NZ's biggest league occasion    NZ Herald
items.body_excerpt:
Peter Brown attempts a kick for the Kiwis during the Rugby League World Cup final against Australia at Eden Park in 1988. Photo / Photosport
For anyone who follows the New Zealand Warriors, there are three conflicting emotions ahead of Sunday’s blockbuster NRL knockout against the Newcastle Knights at Eden Park.
The first is pride. Pride that their club, which was in such a mess for much of the last decade and then almost disappeared during the Covid pandemic, has become the hottest ticket in town, with the almost unprecedented interest in the team.
The second is anticipation. This evening’s match is set up perfectly. A capacity crowd at Eden Park, including many fans who may have struggled to get tickets across this season, yearning to see their heroes.
The Warriors nation will descend on Kingsland, in scenes that might be reminiscent of a mini-Magic Round scenario in Brisbane . It’s also a perfect window for television – on a weekend where there aren’t other major events on – which should ensure a massive broadcast audience.
However, the third emotion is fear. This is the Warriors’ biggest home finals match in years – bigger than the 2023 encounter against the Knights – and they are not at home. Instead, they are at a ground they haven’t played at in more than a decade.
Although some will brush that off, it does matter. Players like familiarity, they thrive on familiarity, especially when times are tough. They know the angles – especially the kickers – which are banked in the memory, while their peripheral vision is enough in the high-pressure moments.
The Warriors at an Eden Park training session. Photo / Photosport.
Being at Eden Park probably helps the Knights. The bigger ground isn’t as intimidating, with a less gladiatorial atmosphere, simply because most of the fans are further away. It’s hard to imagine the same intensity as can be produced at Go Media Stadium (Mt Smart). And while the grand occasion will inspire the Warriors, it also adds pressure; when you sell out the country’s biggest stadium, you need to perform.
However, there is a positive vibe around the club and the players. They have to be positive – otherwise they would be criticised for making excuses, even though they had previously wanted to stay at Go Media for their finals campaign.
But there is now a feeling around the team that this switch could be a tonic, after the sour defeat last week and a couple of middling performances in Penrose across the fortnight before that. Maybe the change of scenery – and the massive support – will be just what the team need, the infusion of energy and excitement that can lift them to new levels.
There is recognition that the Warriors’ past record at Eden Park is poor (played six, won one), though it also understood they were a different team, at a different time (2011-2014) . This team have developed an appetite for big matches, whether it is a sold-out ground in Wellington or Christchurch or the epic battles at Suncorp Stadium.
But NRL finals footy is the biggest challenge. It’s harsh and unforgiving and a few Warriors players simply couldn’t step up last week. They have to this week – in the win-or-bust scenario – though also need to stay calm and focus on the process.
It also needs to be noted that while Sunday should be a tremendous occasion, it will not be, as Eden Park chief executive Nick Saunter tried to claim this week , “the biggest event in league history in New Zealand”. Saunter isn’t afraid of hyperbole and is a brilliant promoter who is always trying to remind everyone of Eden Park’s virtues.
Kiwis legend Mark Graham making a tackle during the 1988 Rugby League World Cup final at Eden Park. Photo / Photosport
But it was strange that he forgot – or didn’t know about – the 1988 Rugby League World Cup final between New Zealand and Australia at Eden Park, which remains, by some distance, the biggest event in league history in this country .

The second NRL Semi Final heads to New Zealand on Sunday afternoon with a thrilling contest between the Warriors and Knights . Before You Bet is here to help find a winner or two with a comprehensive look at what is ahead in this exciting match.

Time to regroup
The Warriors were upset at home 26-16 by the Dolphins, ambushed in the second half of the match as the result slipped away. Unable to build on a strong start which saw them lead 12-8 at HT, injuries at the beginning of the match and suffered throughout hurt their cause. The performance was flat also considering they scored just 1 try, accumulating 10 points via penalty goals. With a greater share of possession (53%), they had a superior completion rate (83%) and ran for 8.5m per carry. Unfortunately, they could only manage 2 line breaks and lacked creativity when it mattered and failed to turn their pressure into points. They were uncharacteristically poor defensively too, missing 54 tackles and allowing 9m per carry.

The Knights caused an upset with a 20-10 road victory over the Rabbitohs. Benefitting from a week off in Round 27, the Knights came out strongly and set a great intensity which they maintained for 80 minutes. Physical on both sides of the ball, they dictated the terms of the match. With a greater share of possession (51%), they completed at 83%, made 9.8m per carry, and had 584 PCM’s. This allowed them to make 6 line breaks, continually breaking the advantage line with their carries. Their defence was also strong, missing just 22 tackles and scrambling well to disrupt their opponent’s momentum.
